field_rule: First find slender aboveground stolons forming a dense mat, then a REAL connected root-emitting node and a pale scaly underground rhizome if available. At the blade/sheath junction find a tiny HAIR-FRINGED MEMBRANOUS rim (about 0.2–0.5 mm) with conspicuous longer collar hairs; the old photo shows the longer hairs, NOT a measured ligule. At bloom look for commonly 4–6 slender terminal ONE-SIDED fingers emerging nearly together. Other fingerhead grasses overlap: check Digitaria's staggered racemes, Eleusine's flattened whitish base, Chloris's separate whorls, and native buffalograss's separate m

head.reference: Usually digitately clustered flowering branches, closely overlapping awnless spikelets.

ligule.source: Kew GrassBase Cynodon dactylon ciliolate membrane versus FNA hair fringe
ligule.reference: Tiny true ligule ~0.2–0.5 mm with cilia may be described as membrane or hair fringe; long side collar hairs are a different structure. Accept existing two broad visual appearances.

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare DIGITATE racemes and individual spikelets
diagnostic_checks.check: Bermudagrass commonly has 4–6 (occasionally more or fewer) thin unilateral racemes radiating from one flowering tip. An individual flattened axis carries one-flowered 2–3 mm spikelets in two close rows; the lemma keel may be SILKY-HIRSŪTE but has no long awn.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Buffalograss male flowerheads can also be comb-like, but females have distinct bur-like head units; goosegrass has 5–7 FLORETS per spikelet and a flattened whitish crown.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase/FNA source-backed; intact flowering fingers and one separated spikelet needed
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Cynodon dactylon

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace both surface STOLONS and buried RHIZOMES
diagnostic_checks.check: A perennial ground mat normally has long creeping SURFACE stolons rooting at joints as well as underground slender SCALY rhizomes. The same plant may have a mat and exposed underground stem, so do not equate bare root with rhizome.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Buffalograss spreads with surface stolons but does not have this same extensive pair of creeping stem systems; curlymesquite shows distinctive white-hairy stolon nodes.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew/FNA morphology; exact underground connecting stem not yet certified in gallery
diagnostic_checks.source: FNA — Cynodon dactylon

diagnostic_checks.look: Find the ligule UNDER the much longer sheath-mouth hairs
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew calls the TRUE ligule a minute (~0.2–0.3 mm) CILIATE MEMBRANE, while FNA emphasizes a ~0.5 mm line/fringe of hairs and often long side collar hairs. Both visible choices can look valid; isolate the inside blade–sheath junction.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Goosegrass has a small erose membrane and different 5–7-flowered spikelets; the outer collar hair tufts alone are not species proof.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew vs FNA wording retained; microscopic same-plant collar pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase / FNA — Cynodon dactylon

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine an entire mature panicle before it breaks away
diagnostic_checks.check: Published GrassBase description gives a very open, broad 25–45 cm panicle with wiry branches; when ripe the panicle may detach and tumble. A purple cloud alone does not distinguish it from other airy lovegrasses.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Plains and sand lovegrass also have transparent panicles but usually retain the head; open heads do not equal identical spikelets.

diagnostic_checks.look: Count florets and view a three-veined lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew gives 5–7 mm long narrow spikelets usually with 7–11 florets; the lower and upper glumes are one-veined, and fertile lemmas are about 1.8–2.2 mm with three veins. Measure an intact mature spikelet.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Red lovegrass has generally larger, compressed and much more multi-flowered spikelets (source subsp. oxylepis variation); purple color alone is not a species ID.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published typical morphology; same-specimen glume, floret and lemma macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Eragrostis spectabilis

diagnostic_checks.look: Open the ligule and trace any knotty underground base
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew calls the ligule a hair fringe; Missouri WeedID instead calls a very short membrane, well under 1 mm. Purple lovegrass may form short KNOTTY rhizomes and a perennial tuft. Image-hair appearance may conceal a minute membrane.
diagnostic_checks.compare: A tufted, non-rhizomatous plains lovegrass can superficially match a purple lovegrass without a flowering head; neither collar nor root alone is decisive.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: SOURCE TERMINOLOGY CONFLICT; hair and membrane are alternative broad field looks, not proof of two biologically separate ligules
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Eragrostis spectabilis (see also Missouri WeedID)

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.202
head.reference: Short 2–3.5 cm spike-like axis bearing 4–8 clusters of THREE spikelets: central fertile and two staminate.

habit.reference: Thin surface stolons join low tufts.

diagnostic_checks.look: Find a real creeping STOLON with hairy rooting nodes
diagnostic_checks.check: Curlymesquite forms low sod by slender, wirelike SURFACE stolons rooting at leafy nodes, usually with a conspicuous tuft of white hairs at some nodes. Often only top 1–2 internodes rise. This is not a buried rhizome.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Tobosa (*Hilaria mutica*) forms stiffer erect tufts from short underground rhizomes; it does not grow a long surface stolon like curlymesquite.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Texas A&M regional account, but exact reference image rooting-node verification pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M — Common curlymesquite

diagnostic_checks.look: Count a THREE-SPIKELET fascicle, not three awns
diagnostic_checks.check: The short roughly 2–3.5 cm spike-like head bears around 4–9 clusters, each a triad: a central fertile spikelet flanked by two generally male/sterile spikelets. Glumes can have short points. A three-spikelet fascicle is NOT three lemma awns from one floret.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Aristida threeawns have one fertile floret with three long terminal awns. Tobosa also has repeated Hilaria triads but larger, more upright perennial growth.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Regional flora and Texas A&M architecture; complete fascicle macro needed
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M — Common curlymesquite

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the tiny membrane and connected turf
diagnostic_checks.check: True inner ligule is a very short lacerate membrane, often about 0.5–1 mm in western US descriptions; do not mistake hairy culm NODES for this ligule. Ground-hugging turf and nodal roots reinforce but do not replace triad inspection.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Tobosa has a ~1 mm lacerate membrane too; neither collar alone identifies a Hilaria species.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Existing regional flora and western description; UT/Texas field sample pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M — Common curlymesquite

head.reference: Detached tumbling head, loosely coiled main axis and few widely spaced spicate branches; existing wiry state confirmed against historical source taxonomy.

habit.reference: Historical treatment confirms tufted perennial 8–50(–70) cm; root connectivity remains unphotographed.

taxonomy.source: Kew POWO accepted Muhlenbergia paniculata; Texas A&M older Schedonnardus paniculatus
taxonomy.reference: Schedonnardus paniculatus is a homotypic synonym of Muhlenbergia paniculata; old synonym shouldn't create another indexed species. One-sided spreading rays can look like wiry or one-sided head. Kew reports annual or perennial in broad range; TAMU Texas perennial.

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the curved main rachis and widely spaced lateral rays
diagnostic_checks.check: Tumblegrass has a curling, scythe-shaped or bent main flowering axis with few (commonly 1–5) long spreading unilateral rays bearing widely spaced spikelets. Whole branched head may break away and tumble at maturity. This is NOT an ordinary open cloud panicle.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Nimblewill has a contracted straight narrow 5–15 cm panicle; other tumbling grasses may have different numbers of florets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Texas A&M and Kew genus under old Schedonnardus; older morphological taxonomy explicit
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M — Tumblegrass (Schedonnardus paniculatus)

diagnostic_checks.look: Open a tiny one-FLORET spikelet attached to its ONE-SIDED ray
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew under historical *Schedonnardus* describes linear 3–4 mm single-floret spikelets SESSILE and appressed to one side of angular ray rachises, falling attached to branch structures. The LOWER glume is about half the upper; not a three-awn floret.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hilaria/Hop three-spikelet clusters contain TWO lateral mostly male spikelets plus a central fertile, not one solitary floret on a unilateral branch.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Genus-level former Schedonnardus morphology, coupled with species field description; exact photo macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase under Schedonnardus in Muhlenbergia genus

diagnostic_checks.look: Keep nomenclature and botanical life cycle separate
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew recognizes *Muhlenbergia paniculata* (2010 combination) and lists *Schedonnardus paniculatus* as its synonym; older Texas A&M resources keep Schedonnardus. Both point to the same tumblegrass. The Texas regional species account calls it perennial, while Kew global distribution says annual OR perennial: local rooted stage still requires checking.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not count historical name as a second species; a detached tumbling seedhead alone cannot determine whether the plant was annual or perennial.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew accepted-name crosswalk and TAMU ecology; local longevity unresolved at range scale
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO — Muhlenbergia paniculata accepted name and synonyms

ligule.reference: Flora treats the ligule as a SHORT SPLITTING FIBROUS MEMBRANE WITH HAIR FRINGE (to 1.3 mm). Either visible hair fringe or membrane can be selected in broad key; not proof of a hair-only structure.

lower_floret.source: Kew GrassBase Panicum hallii vs SW Arizona/New Mexico FNA-style field account
lower_floret.reference: Lower floret consistently sterile in cited sources, but whether lower PALEA is absent/insignificant or nearly full length differs by treatment. Preserve contradiction and do not force a binary palea-presence filter.

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the short-branched head and leaf blades to the rooted base
diagnostic_checks.check: Hall's panicgrass is a tufted perennial with a relatively orderly, ascending 6–20(30) cm panicle and short pedicels that leave close, overlapping small clusters of spikelets. Its older basal blades often curl like wood shavings as they dry.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Kleingrass has more diffusely dispersed smaller spikelets and may have knotty rhizomes; switchgrass is usually tall and strongly rhizomatous.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Texas A&M + FNA; photo of intact flowerhead and basal dry/winter leaves not yet certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M — Hall Panicgrass

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the tiny two-floret spikelet and shiny fertile lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew GrassBase gives ovate 2.2–3.7(3.9) mm spikelets; lower glume ~one-third to two-thirds of their length and mostly FIVE-veined, upper glume reaching the spikelet tip. One basal floret is sterile, and the hardened fertile upper lemma becomes dark, smooth and shiny.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Kleingrass commonly has 2–3.5 mm spikelets and much SHORTER lower glume (~one-quarter to one-third); compare a mature same-scale spikelet and lower floret anatomy.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase and Texas A&M; taxon variety affects spikelet size/branch spreading
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Panicum hallii

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the short ciliate membrane and possible lower floret palea
diagnostic_checks.check: Hall's panicgrass has a very short ciliate membrane (about 0.5–1.5 mm in a regional guide), which can look like hairs. An external NM flora describes the sterile lower floret palea as nearly full length while the GrassBase entry calls it absent or insignificant. Do not build an exclusive filter from this conflict.
diagnostic_checks.compare: P. coloratum has an explicitly STAMINATE (male) lower floret with developed palea; this may be useful under microscopy but needs a true taxon-concept cross-check.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Palea descriptions conflict; record as uncertain, not definitive for specimen ID

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace one bristle to its point of origin
diagnostic_checks.check: A Setaria bristle is a persistent sterile branchlet BELOW the spikelet, not a pointed awn from the lemma. Count the cluster around an intact spikelet: Flora of North America gives usually 4–12 bristles about 2–12 mm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Scheele's bristlegrass usually has one much longer bristle; sandbur spines form a fused burr cup
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; exact attached macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Setaria parviflora

diagnostic_checks.look: Find the living knotty rhizome
diagnostic_checks.check: Perennial plants have short, knotty underground rhizomes and a dense uniform foxtail head about 3–8(10) cm. Show the real connection under the soil, not a detached swollen stem base.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Annual foxtail millet lacks this connected perennial rhizome
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; existing gallery root photo not certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Setaria parviflora

diagnostic_checks.look: Open a spikelet and the INNER collar
diagnostic_checks.check: The hair-fringe ligule is usually less than 1 mm. Spikelets are roughly 2–2.8 mm; upper fertile lemmas are distinctly wrinkled across their width, unlike the smooth/shiny fertile lemmas possible in cultivated millet.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Foxtail millet is much more variable in its large heavy head and has smoother upper lemmas
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; scale and same-plant macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Setaria parviflora

head.reference: Maintains both dense/contracted and loose/open states; narrow green heads are not excluded.

ligule.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, 1999 (user-provided monocots excerpt)
ligule.reference: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Sorghum halepense, printed p.1324: the ligule is membranous with a hair fringe; not an exclusively hair-only ligule.

awns.source: Flora of North America, Sorghum halepense; versus Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas
awns.reference: FNA allows awnless upper fertile lemma OR a geniculate twisted awn to 13 mm. Previous regional-flora 1–1.5 mm statement cannot be a universal cap. Broad key retains both inconspicuous and long-visible awn states.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF page 246
habit.reference: Extensive rhizomes distinguish perennial Johnsongrass from annual S. bicolor.

diagnostic_checks.look: Expose a connected underground rhizome
diagnostic_checks.check: Johnsongrass is a robust perennial producing long, scaly, creeping rhizomes. Keep the connected underground stem attached to a leafy shoot in one photo; a detached white root is not a rhizome.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Sorghum bicolor lacks this extensive persistent rhizome system and is usually annual/short lived
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; existing rhizome photo still needs photo-role QA
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Sorghum halepense

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine a sessile AND its pedicelled companion spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: A Johnsongrass branch ends in short spikelet-pair rames; FNA describes a fertile sessile spikelet about 3.8–6.5 mm and a developed pedicelled mostly staminate companion about 3.6–5.6 mm. This is NOT an empty pedicel as in Indiangrass.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Sorghastrum nutans has only a bare companion pedicel; Sorghum bicolor has heavier often persistent grain-bearing spikelets
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; paired unit macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Sorghum halepense

diagnostic_checks.look: Do not force Johnsongrass to be awnless
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA permits a mature sessile spikelet lemma either without an awn OR with a twisted, bent awn up to about 13 mm. Examine the true blade–sheath junction: membrane 2–6 mm with a ciliate edge.
diagnostic_checks.compare: S. bicolor can also be awnless or long-awned, so this is a safe filter state rather than stand-alone diagnosis
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA regional contrast with older North Central Texas short-awn claim: retain both options
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Sorghum halepense

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas pp.166–167
head.reference: Species complex includes contracted and open panicles across named varieties; do not require one universally airy head.

glumes.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase Aristida purpurea (species account); concept varies by infraspecific name
glumes.reference: Lower glume about 6–8 mm, usually 1-veined; upper about 11–15 mm. Compare A. oligantha lower glume normally 3–7-veined. Do not apply as universal cutoffs to every A. purpurea variety.

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare the lengths and veins of both glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: In GrassBase's typical species account, the LOWER glume is roughly 6–8 mm and one-veined, versus an UPPER glume about 11–15 mm and one-veined. Measurements can differ among varieties: record the taxon concept.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Prairie threeawn has a longer 3–7-veined lower glume usually closer to the upper glume length
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published typical-species measurements, not universal variety cutoffs
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Aristida purpurea

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the perennial crown and a mature floret
diagnostic_checks.check: Purple threeawn is a perennial rooted tuft; mature florets normally show three spreading awns arising from ONE lemma. A purple color or a narrow panicle by itself does not confirm this species.
diagnostic_checks.compare: A. oligantha is annual; its three long awns can look very similar at a distance
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase and broad FNA genus morphology; root/photo QA pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Aristida purpurea
